ISciences Water Security Indicator Model (WSIM) November 19, 2026 This month’s In Focus looks deeper into: The super El Niño solidifies, with Pacific temperatures “off the monitoring charts”Record tides and flooding across the western United StatesA deepening food crisis in Central America’s Dry Corridor In Focus El Niño Reaches Uncharted Territory El Niño crossed a historic threshold in October. The Copernicus Climate Change Service reported that the monthly average sea surface temperature in the Niño 3.4 region reached an all-time high of 29.94 °C, an anomaly of 3.21 °C that exceeded the peaks of the very strong 1982–1983, 1997–1998, and 2015–2016 events. WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo described conditions as “literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades.” The warming does not appear to be finished. Zeke Hausfather’s analysis for Carbon Brief of more than 600 forecasts from 14 climate models points to a peak near 4 °C, with 10 of the 14 models placing it in December, and NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center expects strengthening through the end of the year. The three-month Relative Oceanic Niño Index of 1.97 °C for August–October ranks second for that period since 1950 , behind only 1997. The NOAA CFSv2 ensemble that drives WSIM’s forecasts is shown here on the relative Niño 3.4 index ( Figure 1 ). On this index, observed values reached about 2.5 °C in October. The ensemble mean peaks near 2.7 °C in November, slightly below last month’s projection of 2.8 to 2.9 °C, and holds near 2.5 °C through January before declining steadily. It falls below 0.5 °C by around May 2027 and dips just below zero by July. Even before the event peaks, El Niño’s effects have already arrived across the Americas as record floods, extraordinary tides, and deepening drought.
